An alcove is a small, recessed section built into or carved out of a larger space — most commonly a room or a wall. Think of it as a sheltered "pocket" or "nook" that is set back from the main area around it. It is always part of a bigger structure, never a standalone space.

The single most important feature of an alcove is that it is recessed — meaning it is pushed inward, deeper than the surrounding surface. Imagine standing in a room and noticing that one section of the wall doesn't lie flat. Instead, it goes further back, creating a small, sheltered space. That is an alcove.

Picture a rectangular room. Now imagine that one section of the wall has been "pushed back," creating a small pocket-like space. This pocket has walls on three sides and is open on the fourth side, which faces the main room. That is the classic shape of an alcove.

Alcoves vary in size. Some are small — just deep enough to hold a vase or a statue on a shelf. Others are large enough for a person to sit in comfortably, with a cushioned seat, a small desk, or even a bed tucked inside.

In rooms: Bedrooms sometimes have sleeping alcoves, where the bed sits in a recessed space, making the room feel cozy and private. Living rooms may have a reading alcove — a small recessed corner with a cushioned bench or an armchair where one can sit and read. Restaurants often design dining alcoves to give small groups a sense of privacy from the larger, busier room around them.

In walls and corridors: A hallway might have an alcove cut into the wall where a water fountain, a sculpture, or a telephone is placed. Libraries and museums often feature alcoves along their corridors to display artwork or provide seating without blocking foot traffic.

Outdoors: In gardens, an alcove can be a shaded, recessed nook formed by hedges, stone walls, or an archway — a quiet, sheltered spot to sit, set apart from the open space around it.

Alcoves are almost always associated with a sense of coziness, intimacy, and shelter. Because they are set apart from the main open space, they feel more private and enclosed. This is precisely why they are popular for reading spots, private dining, and decorative displays — they create a special, well-defined area within a larger space and naturally draw the eye toward them.
How It Differs from Similar Words

Niche: Very close in meaning, but a niche is generally smaller and shallower — usually just a hollow in a wall for displaying a decorative object like a statue. You would not sit inside a niche. An alcove tends to be larger and more usable.

Nook: A warm, informal, everyday word for a small cozy corner or recess. "Alcove" is the more precise, architectural term for the same general idea.

Bay (as in bay window): A section of a room that juts outward from the building's exterior wall. An alcove goes inward. They are essentially opposite in direction.

Annex or extension: A full addition to a building or room — much larger and more room-like than an alcove.

• "She curled up in the window alcove with a book and a cup of tea."
  • "The museum corridor had small alcoves displaying ancient Greek sculptures."
  • "The architect designed a sleeping alcove to save space in the studio apartment."
  • "In the garden, they built a stone alcove with a bench, sheltered from the wind."
  • "The children liked to hide in the alcove behind the staircase."

An alcove is a small, recessed, three-walled space that is set back into a room, wall, or outdoor structure, open on one side toward the larger space it belongs to, and associated with a feeling of coziness, shelter, and privacy.
